title: Prompt 22 — Agent Loop Lab: Read, Calculate and Verify

scenes.title: A real application
scenes.text: Welcome to Prompt twenty two: the agent loop. In this lesson, we will run a real TypeScript application with the Claude Agent SDK. You will see the input file, an actual tool call, the model result, and the independent check that decides whether to save a report.

scenes.title: The original lesson map
scenes.text: Here is our original infographic. The task is to read a file, perform a calculation, and report the result. Keep this distinction in mind: the SDK manages model turns and tool execution. Our application prepares the input, restricts the permitted file, validates the answer, and saves the report. We will now connect these ideas to working code.

scenes.title: Prepare a real file
scenes.text: The application starts with five integers: twelve, eight, fifteen, five, and ten. Their total is fifty, their minimum is five, and their maximum is fifteen. Each run writes a separate values dot text file. The orange button starts a live Claude run. Verify locally uses ordinary application code and makes no model request. These are separate modes so that students can check the calculation without spending API credit.

scenes.title: Configure the runtime
scenes.text: Open agent dot TypeScript. These are the actual files used by this application. The options select a model, set the run directory, and expose the built in Read tool. Project settings and MCP servers are disabled for this small lesson. Four turns and a fifty cent budget limit the run. The working directory provides context; it is not, by itself, a filesystem security boundary. Our code adds a specific permission check.

scenes.title: Restrict the input file
scenes.text: The permission check resolves the real input path, then compares it with the requested Read path. A different file is denied. This is an application policy for the exposed tool, rather than an operating system sandbox. The SDK also adds Structured Output when a JSON schema is requested. We allow that formatting tool explicitly because it does not read files. The final statistics still have to pass independent validation.

scenes.title: Consume the SDK stream
scenes.text: Query starts the agent, and the for await loop consumes the SDK message stream. We are not manually calling Read and pretending that Claude chose it. Claude requests the tool, the SDK runs it, and the tool result becomes an observation for a subsequent model turn. Initialization gives us the actual model and session. A successful result supplies structured output. Tool hooks provide the separate evidence shown in the timeline.

scenes.title: Run Claude on the real input
scenes.text: Now we click Run live Claude agent. Watch the observed events rather than assuming that a successful API request proves the task is complete. The application saves the input and checks its format. The SDK initializes the session. Claude then requests Read for this run's file. After the observation returns, the model can calculate its answer. The application waits for the result, compares every statistic with its reference calculation, and only then writes a verified report.

scenes.title: Inspect the actual Read result
scenes.text: Expand the Read observation. This is the tool response captured by the SDK hook during the recorded run. It contains the five lines from the input file. The tool request and response share a tool use identifier, so we can connect the action with its observation. This timeline shows observable events, not a reconstruction of the model's private reasoning. We require a completed Read before accepting this lesson's agent result.

scenes.title: Verify the result
scenes.text: The report shows five numbers, a total of fifty, a minimum of five, and a maximum of fifteen. The badge says Claude result verified because the model's four values matched an independent calculation. The evidence also records the model, the observed Read count, and a hash of the exact input. Correct arithmetic does not establish reliability for every possible task. It gives us a concrete acceptance check for this particular lesson.

scenes.title: Inspect the saved evidence
scenes.text: Open the report details and compare expected with actual. Both objects must match. The JSON download contains the structured report, while the Markdown download is a readable summary. Execution evidence downloads the observed event log. These are real files written by the application. When you reproduce this lesson, your session identifier, timestamps, and API cost will differ. Check the input and verified values rather than copying the recording's metadata.

scenes.title: Reject incorrect arithmetic
scenes.text: The validator requires an object with safe integer values. It checks count, total, minimum, and maximum against the independently calculated reference. If the model returned fifty one instead of fifty, this comparison would reject the result. The application does not publish that answer as a verified report. The unit tests deliberately inject an incorrect model result to exercise this failure path. A test double is useful for this check; it is separate from the live Claude run you just watched.

scenes.title: Show a meaningful failure
scenes.text: Let's introduce a real input error. In the second sample, line three contains the word fifteen instead of an integer. Click the live button again. Preflight validation stops the run before the SDK is called. The message identifies line three, the previous statistics are cleared, and no verified report is offered. This behavior matters: a stale successful result must not look like the result of a failed request.

scenes.title: Repair and verify locally
scenes.text: Select the valid sample to repair the input, then choose Verify locally. The total returns to fifty, but the badge explicitly says Local verifier only. There is no Claude call in this step. This gives students a fast way to check input parsing and arithmetic before spending time on a model run. Use the live mode when you need to observe the SDK's actual tool execution and subsequent result.

scenes.title: Practice and acceptance checks
scenes.text: Your exercise is to replace the sample with minus four, six, and zero, one number per line. Before running it, predict the answer: count three, total two, minimum minus four, maximum six. Start with local verification, then run Claude and compare the evidence. Finally, try a decimal or an empty file and explain why no report is saved. The downloadable project includes setup instructions, tests, and the exercise solution.

scenes.title: What the agent loop means
scenes.text: You have now connected the infographic to a working application: a real input file, an observed Read request and observation, a structured model result, and a verified report. The SDK supplies the agent loop. Your application supplies the acceptance criteria and the handling of errors. In your own project, define what success means before you rely on the final answer, and keep the evidence that lets you check it.
